opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the core issue is that a lot of these frameworks were designed in a world where you'd evaluate a model by giving it a fixed prompt and looking at a single response. The implicit assumption was that the model you test is roughly the capability ceiling of what you're releasing. But with reasoning models, that assumption breaks down. The capability of the system isn't fixed at training time anymore; it scales with how much compute you let it spend thinking at inference.

So if you run your dangerous-capability evals at some modest thinking budget and conclude the model is below a threshold, that might not tell you much about what happens when someone lets it think ten times or a hundred times longer, or runs many samples and picks the best one. You can get a meaningfully more capable system out of the same weights just by spending more at test time.

What I'd like to see is frameworks that treat test-time compute as a first-class axis. Instead of asking "is this model dangerous?", ask "at what level of inference compute does this model cross a given threshold?" Then you're tracking a curve rather than a single point, and you can extrapolate. If the capability keeps going up as you scale thinking time, you should take that seriously, because the cost of inference keeps coming down, so what's expensive today might be cheap and widely accessible in a year.

I don't think this is an unsolvable problem. It's mostly that evaluation practices haven't fully caught up with the paradigm shift. Labs that do this well will elicit capabilities as aggressively as a determined user would, including with long reasoning budgets, and set their thresholds accordingly.

r001.rationale: The response says system capability scales with the amount of compute spent thinking at inference and that more test-time compute can produce a more capable system from the same weights.

r002.rationale: It describes frameworks built around a fixed prompt and single response, then says they should treat test-time compute as a first-class axis and evaluate the level at which capabilities cross a threshold. This identifies the missing compute-budget dimension for dangerous-capability evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that most of these frameworks were designed around a world where capability was basically a fixed property of a model. You train a model, you run your evals on it, you get a number, and that number tells you what the model can and can't do. And that made sense when scaling was almost entirely about pretraining. The model you shipped was the model you evaluated.

But that's not the world we're in anymore. With test-time compute, capability isn't a point, it's a curve. The same set of weights can look very different depending on how much you let it think, how many samples you draw, whether you're doing search or verification on top of it. So when a lab says "we evaluated this model and it's below the threshold for, say, bio or cyber uplift," the honest question is: evaluated at what compute budget? Because if you ran it for ten times longer, or a hundred times longer, you might get a meaningfully different answer. And in a lot of these frameworks, that question just isn't addressed, or it's addressed with a default inference setting that bears no relation to what a motivated adversary would actually do.

That's the part that worries me. The threat model for misuse is not someone using the product at default settings. It's someone who's willing to spend a lot of money on inference to get one really good answer. And we've seen this pattern over and over in my own work. In poker, in Diplomacy, in the reasoning models, the gap between a cheap forward pass and a system that's allowed to deliberate is enormous. It's not a few percentage points. It can be the difference between a system that's essentially useless on a hard problem and one that solves it.

So the fix, I think, is pretty conceptually simple even if it's hard operationally. You have to evaluate at the frontier of compute you're willing to make available, not at the average. You have to treat an eval result as conditional on a budget, and you have to extrapolate. If you can see that performance on a dangerous capability eval is climbing steadily as you add inference compute, you shouldn't be taking comfort in where the curve happens to be at the budget you tested. You should be asking where it's going. And honestly, the labs are the only ones with a clear view of those scaling curves, so there's a real responsibility there to be upfront about them rather than reporting the number that happens to clear the bar.

r001.rationale: The response says capability varies with how much the same model is allowed to think and with the inference compute allocated.

r002.rationale: It says safety frameworks often do not address the compute budget used for evaluation, or rely on a default inference setting.

astra-6.text:
I think the central problem is that you’re not evaluating a fixed level of capability anymore. How capable a model is depends on how much compute you give it at test time. You can evaluate it with one budget and conclude that it’s below some threshold, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you what happens if somebody gives it ten or a hundred times as much compute.

So the question shouldn’t just be, “Did this model pass our safety evaluations?” It should be, “How does its performance on those evaluations change as we increase test-time compute?” And what budget are we assuming someone could realistically use? Otherwise, you risk treating a limitation of the evaluation budget as a limitation of the model.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says a model’s capability depends on how much test-time compute it receives.

r002.rationale: It says evaluations should ask what compute budget is being assumed and warns that otherwise a budget limit may be mistaken for a model limit, conveying that the evaluation budget needs to be specified.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central problem is that you can’t really evaluate a model’s capabilities independently of how much compute you give it at test time. A model might fail a safety evaluation when it has a small budget to work on each problem, but succeed when you let it reason for much longer or make many attempts.

So if a lab says, “We tested this model, and it falls below our threshold for a dangerous capability,” the question is: under what compute budget? And how does that compare with what somebody could actually spend using the model?

The evaluation needs to account for that scaling. Otherwise, you risk interpreting a limitation of the testing setup as a limitation of the model.

r001.rationale: The response says capability evaluations can change when a model gets more test-time compute, such as a longer reasoning budget or more attempts.

r002.rationale: It asks what compute budget applies when a lab reports a model below a dangerous-capability threshold, identifying that the evaluation budget needs to be specified.
